title: Perfect joy
hook: Francis says perfect joy is being turned away cold and wet and staying patient (Little Flowers 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lady Poverty: Francis's bride, freedom from owning. Your line was free of things. What did you give away, and how did your hands feel after? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

Winter. Two friars are walking a long road in bitter cold, Brother Leo out in front and Francis behind. Francis calls ahead. Brother Leo, write this down. If our brothers everywhere set a great example of holiness, that is not perfect joy. A little further on he calls again. If a brother healed the sick and gave sight to the blind, write it down: that is not perfect joy. Again. If he knew every language, and all the scriptures, and could tell the future, not perfect joy. If he preached so well that unbelievers turned to God, not perfect joy. On and on, down the road, until at last Leo, amazed, asks: Father, then tell me, what is perfect joy?

Francis answers with a scene. We arrive at our own friary at night, soaked with rain, stiff with cold, spattered with mud and hungry, and we knock at the gate. The brother on the door says, Who are you? We say, two of your brothers. And he says, You're lying. You're a pair of tramps who go around fooling people and taking the alms of the poor. Go away. And he leaves us outside in the snow and the rain. If we bear that patiently, Francis says, without grumbling, and think that perhaps this porter knows us as we truly are, write it down, Brother Leo: that is perfect joy. The story pushes further. They knock again and are driven off; again, and are beaten. Still: perfect joy. Why? Francis gives the reason himself. Everything on his first list, the example, the healings, the languages, the preaching, is God's gift, so nobody can boast of it. He quotes Paul: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" The one thing a person can bring of their own is to bear a hard thing patiently, for love of Christ. And he quotes Paul again: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." This isn't a call to stay in harm's way. It's a story about pride. The usual move, shut out in the rain, is to rehearse the speech: do you know who I am? Francis's joy is not needing to win that argument. Yesterday he was free of things. Today he's free of his own reputation.
screen: `NOTHING OF OUR OWN TO BOAST OF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay patient in one rejection. Sit, and recall a recent time you were turned away or brushed off. A message ignored. A flat no. Someone who didn't believe you. Notice the old speech start up: the defense, the comeback. Don't deliver it. Let it run out, like rain off a roof. If you pray, you can hold that moment before God with Paul's line: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? If you don't, just breathe, and let the door stay shut. The bell holds the time.
Perfect joy. Francis's name for bearing a hard rejection patiently, for love, with nothing to prove.
Your line: perfect joy. Today, if someone shuts a door on you, even a small one, skip the speech once. Stay patient, and see what's left. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians tell the story of perfect joy from the Little Flowers of St Francis as a lesson in humility and patience; the story itself ends with Paul's words about glorying only in the cross.

fork.setup: you're Francis, soaked and frozen at your own friary gate. the porter calls you a liar and shuts you out. what does Francis call perfect joy?
options: pound on the gate until he lets you in.
go and tell the other brothers what he did.
fork.reveal: bearing it patiently, even thinking the porter may know you truly: write it down, Brother Leo, that is perfect joy.

original.note: Italian, not Latin: perfect joy, as the Little Flowers (Fioretti) names it.

trapdoor: what you thought: perfect joy is everything going your way.
what it means: bearing a cold, shut gate patiently, for love, without needing to win.
what a scholar hears: Little Flowers 8 grounds it in Paul: gifts are received, so no boasting; glory only in the cross.

notes: Little Flowers ch. 8 paraphrased throughout: the road (in the story, from Perugia to St Mary of the Angels), the list of what is not perfect joy, the porter, and the repeated knocking ending in a beating. Some items on the list are trimmed (e.g. raising the dead). Confirm order: in the story Leo walks ahead and Francis calls to him.
'and could tell the future' summarizes the gift of prophecy on Francis's list; confirm.
Paul quotations: the Little Flowers has Francis cite 1 Corinthians 4:7 and Galatians 6:14 (in its own wording); the script uses the KJV. Confirm.
'This isn't a call to stay in harm's way' is an editorial guard so the story of being beaten isn't read as advice to tolerate abuse; confirm it fits.
Original: 'perfetta letizia' is the Italian of the Fioretti; confirm.
Editor pass: 'until Leo can't bear it' overstated Leo's state in Little Flowers 8 (he asks in wonder); now 'until at last Leo, amazed, asks'.

Audit: teach screen head 'WHAT HAST THOU NOT RECEIVED?' misquoted 1 Corinthians 4:7 (KJV: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?); replaced with an unquoted head, 'NOTHING OF OUR OWN TO BOAST OF'.
